summary: Gifford Pinchot NF, Skamania County, WA; a D-6 cupola cabin from about 1920, L-4 towers of the 1930s and 1941, a 1970 removal, and no source describing the site today.

facts.design: D-6 cupola cabin (1920s), then wooden L-4 tower(s); FFLOS says one 20-foot L-4 tower from 1941, FireLookout.com and Willhite say 10-foot L-4 towers
facts.status_note: Tower removed in 1970 per FFLOS and Willhite; FireLookout.com says destroyed in 1970.

events.note: Newspaper notice said a lookout would be provided on the mountain that summer; Willhite says the cabin was likely delayed about a year
D-6 cupola cabin, per Willhite; an August 1920 Spokesman-Review story describes a standard lookout house finished on the summit. FFLOS dates the cabin only to the 1920s

During August 1927 fires on the Columbia National Forest a newspaper said the Siouxon, Gumboot and Lookout Mountain stations were believed likely to burn and the instruments removed and houses abandoned

Lightning set an old snag no more than 150 feet from the lookout cabin on fire on August 29; the lookout reported it and a five-person crew from Co. 605 put it out that evening. A Lookout Mountain Camp was in operation at this time
In a 2002 interview, Pete Paladeni recalled CCC camp work near Lookout Mountain in 1934 and said he was stationed at the lookout about three weeks
FFLOS: a 20-foot wooden L-4 tower replaced the cabin in 1941. FireLookout.com lists a 10-foot L-4 tower dated 1941 with a question mark. Willhite places a second 10-foot L-4 cab in the early 1940s
Forest Service said regular air patrols were expected to take over detection work from its lookouts; Lookout Mountain was one of six stations retained, mainly for communications coverage
Tower removed per FFLOS and Willhite; FireLookout.com says destroyed
Registered June 24, 2012 as US 1328, WA 228; nominated by Ray Kresek

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS describes a 20-foot L-4 tower replacing the cabin in 1941; FireLookout.com and Willhite describe 10-foot L-4 towers in the 1930s and early 1940s. The story reports both and does not choose.
FFLOS and Willhite say the tower was removed in 1970; FireLookout.com says destroyed. The date 1970 agrees across all three.

notes_for_editor: No source read describes the summit today, what remains there, or public access; the access level is left out rather than guessed. The Weebly page is a compilation of newspaper quotes and its 1933 report is a camp fire report, not a newspaper. The 1934 staffing is from a 2002 interview as summarized by Willhite. Brief's elevation (1286.9 m) matches FFLOS (1,287 m).
